log.text: Searching for prior work that already answers each gap

risks: Two seeds may be insufficient to observe a reliable crossover point in the accuracy-gap curves
The non-augmented model may not overfit within 30 epochs on Fashion-MNISTs 60K training set requiring even longer runs
Effect sizes may be below 0.5% throughout making any conclusions highly uncertain
gaps.title: Augmentation benefit direction in 5-epoch underfitting regime

impact.why: Answers a practically important question about when augmentation is worth applying under compute-constrained training.

novelty.why: None of the prior work specifically investigates whether geometric augmentation is neutral or harmful at very short training runs (~5 epochs) versus beneficial at longer runs on Fashion-MNIST with a small CNN; the closest works (e.g., 'State-of-the-Art Results with the Fashion-MNIST Dataset' and 'Multi-Class Image Classification on Fashion-MNIST') use augmentation with longer training schedules (20–100 epochs) without studying the epoch-regime dependency of augmentation benefit.

feasibility.why: Directly extends the core study protocol with only additional epoch-count variants on the same infrastructure.

testability.why: Accuracy at each epoch count is a fully determinate numerical outcome with a clear comparison criterion.

gaps.approach: Run the core 5-epoch protocol for both conditions with seeds 42 and 123, then extend training to 10, 20, and 30 epochs using the same seeds and architecture. Record test accuracy and training/validation loss at each endpoint. Plot the accuracy gap (augmented minus non-augmented) as a function of epoch count to determine whether 5 epochs falls in a regime where augmentation is neutral or harmful and identify the epoch at which consistent benefits first appear.
gaps.question: Does basic geometric augmentation improve or degrade test accuracy of a small CNN trained for only approximately 5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST, where underfitting rather than overfitting is likely to dominate?
gaps.why_open: Studies demonstrating augmentation benefits such as (Çetiner et al. 2023) and (Imam et al. 2026) train models for 50–200 epochs on CIFAR-10 where overfitting dominates, making their results inapplicable to the 5-epoch underfitting regime. (Lin et al. 2023) explicitly shows augmentation can degrade performance when underfitting occurs but does not quantify this effect for Fashion-MNIST or short training budgets. (Guo 2024) shows that even LeNet-5 achieves only 90% validation accuracy on Fashion-MNIST at similar training lengths, suggesting small CNNs operate in a capacity-limited regime where augmentation may introduce harmful noise rather than beneficial regularisation.
gaps.hypothesis: At 5 epochs of training a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST has insufficient capacity utilisation for augmentation to provide a regularisation benefit, resulting in equal or lower test accuracy for the augmented condition, with the benefit emerging only after 15–25 epochs when the non-augmented model begins overfitting.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST via torchvision (60K train, 10K test); no additional data required

gaps.title: Ablation of individual augmentation components on Fashion-MNIST

impact.why: Identifying which single augmentation technique provides most benefit avoids unnecessary noise and compute overhead.

novelty.why: A Preliminary Study on Data Augmentation (2019) examines how augmentation method combinations affect CNN classification accuracy and finds that combining two geometric methods can degrade performance—directly relevant to the proposed hypothesis—but does so on different datasets and does not isolate flip, crop, and rotation on Fashion-MNIST in the structured ablation proposed. The specific dataset, architecture, and the full factorial design across all seven conditions remain unaddressed.

feasibility.why: Defining additional training conditions with different torchvision transform pipelines is trivially easy in PyTorch.

testability.why: Each augmentation condition produces a scalar test accuracy making the comparison direct and fully reproducible.

gaps.approach: Define seven augmentation conditions: no augmentation, flip only, crop only, rotation only, flip+crop, flip+rotation, crop+rotation, and all three combined. Run each condition for 5 epochs with seeds 42 and 123 on the same small CNN. Report test accuracy for all conditions in a summary table, compute the marginal contribution of each technique as the accuracy change from adding it to the full combination, and test whether any combination exceeds the best single-technique condition.
gaps.question: When horizontal flip, random crop, and rotation are each applied individually versus in all pairwise and full combinations, which technique drives accuracy gains for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST at 5 epochs, and does combining techniques improve over the best single technique?
gaps.why_open: (Çetiner et al. 2023) explicitly finds that combining augmentation techniques on CIFAR-10 does not improve over individual techniques and notes the reasons are not analysed. (Korzhebin et al. 2021) confirms that the combination of individually best methods does not necessarily achieve the best combined result but uses only 40 training images. (Shijie et al. 2017) ranks individual augmentation techniques on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet but does not study their interactions or apply them to Fashion-MNIST. No study has performed a systematic single-technique and combination ablation of flip, crop, and rotation specifically on Fashion-MNIST with a small CNN.
gaps.hypothesis: Horizontal flip alone drives the majority of the combined augmentation benefit on Fashion-MNIST because fashion items have meaningful left-right symmetry, while random crop and rotation each add limited additional benefit and their combination with flip produces no statistically meaningful improvement over flip alone.

The specific dataset, architecture, and the full factorial design across all seven conditions remain unaddressed.

gaps.title: Minimum seeds for reliable augmentation comparison: variance characterisation

impact.why: Establishing a minimum seed recommendation would materially improve reproducibility standards for augmentation benchmarking.

novelty.why: None of the prior works directly measure run-to-run test accuracy variance for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST nor conduct a formal power analysis to determine the number of seeds needed to detect augmentation benefits at a specified statistical power level; the closest work on augmentation comparisons (e.g., 'Comparison of simple augmentation transformations') focuses on which augmentation works best across datasets, not on seed-count requirements or sampling variance characterization.

feasibility.why: Many short 5-epoch runs are feasible on Colab but require multi-session management for 60 total runs.

testability.why: Standard deviation and the resulting power curve are fully determined by observed data with a clear numerical output.

gaps.approach: Run 30 seeds for both the augmented and non-augmented conditions (5 epochs each) on the small CNN with all other hyperparameters fixed. Compute the mean and standard deviation of test accuracy across seeds, plot the empirical sampling distribution, and perform a power analysis using the observed standard deviation to determine the minimum n required to detect effect sizes of 0.1%, 0.5%, and 1% at 80% power. Report a concrete seed-count recommendation for future augmentation benchmarking studies on this task.
gaps.question: How large is the run-to-run test accuracy variance for a small CNN trained on Fashion-MNIST for 5 epochs, and how many random seeds are required to detect a typical augmentation benefit with 80% statistical power?
gaps.why_open: The core study's documented limitation is that two seeds are insufficient for statistical significance testing and it is unclear how much run-to-run variance should be expected, yet no paper explicitly characterises seed-to-seed accuracy variance for this specific setting. (Sayın et al. 2025) applies two-way ANOVA across optimizer-activation combinations on Fashion-MNIST but reports aggregate statistics rather than per-seed distributions for augmentation comparisons. Without an empirical variance estimate the minimum number of seeds needed to reliably compare augmented and non-augmented conditions cannot be principled.
gaps.hypothesis: The run-to-run standard deviation in test accuracy for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST at 5 epochs lies between 0.1% and 0.5%, requiring at least 8–20 seeds per condition to detect a 0.5% augmentation benefit with 80% power using a paired t-test.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST via torchvision (60K train, 10K test); same architecture and hyperparameters as the core study

risks: With only 2 seeds per-class estimates are highly noisy and statistical conclusions are unreliable
Per-class effect sizes may be below 1% and dominated by seed variance rather than augmentation
Class-level results may be specific to the chosen small CNN architecture
gaps.title: Per-class accuracy differential under augmentation for confusable classes

impact.why: Provides mechanistic insight into augmentation effects at class level but is a secondary analysis with limited practical consequence.

novelty.why: None of the prior works examine per-class augmentation benefit specifically for visually confusable versus easily separable categories on Fashion-MNIST, nor do they apply a cluster-level statistical test (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank) to compare augmentation gains across garment similarity groups.

feasibility.why: Requires only confusion matrix extraction from runs already performed in the core study with no additional GPU time.

testability.why: Per-class F1 differences are deterministic given model predictions though statistical power with 2 seeds is limited.

gaps.approach: From the core study's 4 training runs extract per-class precision recall and F1 score from confusion matrices at the final epoch for all 10 Fashion-MNIST categories. Compute the per-class accuracy difference (augmented minus non-augmented) for each category across both seeds. Rank classes by magnitude of augmentation benefit and apply a Wilcoxon signed-rank test to assess whether the confusable garment cluster shows systematically larger gains than the footwear and accessories cluster.
gaps.question: Does basic geometric augmentation disproportionately improve classification accuracy for visually confusable Fashion-MNIST classes such as shirt, coat, and pullover compared with easily separable classes such as sandal, bag, and ankle boot?
gaps.why_open: All augmentation papers surveyed including (Çetiner et al. 2023), (Imam et al. 2026), (Shijie et al. 2017), (Gu et al. 2019), and (Helmud et al. 2024) report only aggregate test accuracy or macro-averaged metrics, providing no insight into which categories benefit most from augmentation. Fashion-MNIST is known to have a cluster of visually confusable upper-body garments driving most classification errors, as evidenced by per-class difficulty patterns implicit in models reported in (Vattikonda, et al. 2024) and (Ahmad et al. 2026), but no study has measured augmentation's per-class effect to determine whether it differentially helps confusable versus separable categories.
gaps.hypothesis: Augmentation produces larger per-class accuracy gains for confusable garment categories (shirt, coat, pullover, T-shirt/top) than for easily separable categories (sandal, bag, ankle boot) because geometric transformations expand intra-class variability that helps the model learn invariant features specifically for visually similar items.
gaps.data_needed: Per-class predictions and confusion matrices from the core study 4 training runs; no additional training required

gaps.title: Training data size threshold for positive augmentation effect

impact.why: Directly guides practitioners working with limited labelled data on whether to invest in augmentation pipelines.

novelty.why: None of the prior works specifically investigate the crossover threshold at which basic geometric augmentation transitions from neutral/negative to positive accuracy gain as a function of training set size for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST; the closest work (Purposive Data Augmentation Strategy) touches on augmentation in small-sample industrial datasets but does not characterize a crossover threshold or use a controlled subsampling approach on a benchmark image classification dataset.

feasibility.why: Stratified subsampling and multiple conditions are straightforward in PyTorch and fit within Colab GPU limits.

testability.why: The crossover dataset size is a measurable quantity though only 2 seeds per size introduces uncertainty in locating it precisely.

gaps.approach: Subsample the Fashion-MNIST training set at seven sizes (500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 30000, 60000) using stratified sampling. For each size run both augmented and non-augmented conditions for 5 epochs using seeds 42 and 123. Plot mean accuracy gain versus training size and fit a piecewise-linear or sigmoid curve to locate the crossover point where augmentation transitions from net-negative to net-positive.
gaps.question: What minimum training set size causes basic geometric augmentation to shift from a neutral or negative effect to a consistently positive accuracy gain for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST at 5 epochs?
gaps.why_open: (Lin et al. 2023) demonstrates that augmentation can degrade performance below a dataset-size threshold but does not quantify that threshold and uses an unnamed dataset. (Shijie et al. 2017) notes augmentation gains are more pronounced on smaller datasets but only compares two scale levels rather than sweeping systematically. (Anusree et al. 2026) shows a 9.11% gain on Fashion-MNIST with only 50 samples per class using chaotic transformations, confirming size effects exist but not pinpointing a crossover for standard geometric augmentation. No study has conducted a systematic size sweep on Fashion-MNIST to determine at what N simple augmentation becomes reliably beneficial.
gaps.hypothesis: Basic geometric augmentation yields negligible or negative accuracy gains at the full 60K training set due to sufficient data diversity, but produces measurable positive gains below approximately 5000 training samples, with the crossover threshold occurring somewhere between 5K and 15K samples.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST via torchvision with stratified subsampling implemented in PyTorch

closest.title: Purposive Data Augmentation Strategy and Lightweight Classification Model for Small Sample Industrial Defect Dataset
closest.overlap: Examines data augmentation effectiveness on small-sample imbalanced datasets with a lightweight CNN, but focuses on class-targeted augmentation strategy rather than identifying a sample-size crossover threshold for geometric augmentation.

novelty_check.explanation: None of the prior works specifically investigate the crossover threshold at which basic geometric augmentation transitions from neutral/negative to positive accuracy gain as a function of training set size for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST; the closest work (Purposive Data Augmentation Strategy) touches on augmentation in small-sample industrial datasets but does not characterize a crossover threshold or use a controlled subsampling approach on a benchmark image classification dataset.

gaps.title: Augmentation hyperparameter sensitivity grid on Fashion-MNIST

impact.why: Knowing which augmentation parameters matter helps set defaults for future studies but has limited theoretical novelty.

novelty.why: None of the prior works perform a systematic sensitivity analysis or factorial grid search over flip probability, crop fraction, and rotation angle as isolated parameters on Fashion-MNIST with a small CNN at ~5 epochs; the closest works apply augmentation as a fixed preprocessing step without ablating individual parameter values.

feasibility.why: 27 conditions with a single seed is manageable but risks exceeding Colab session limits and conflates noise with hyperparameter effects.

testability.why: Each condition yields a scalar accuracy and an ANOVA decomposition provides a clear quantitative answer about sensitivity.

gaps.approach: Design a full 3-factor grid: flip_prob in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} times crop_fraction in {0.05, 0.10, 0.20} times rotation_deg in {5, 10, 20} yielding 27 conditions. Run each condition for 5 epochs with seed 42 on the small CNN. Report accuracy as a 3D response surface, compute main effects and two-way interactions via ANOVA decomposition, and identify which augmentation parameter has the largest influence on accuracy within the tested range.
gaps.question: How sensitive is the accuracy gain from geometric augmentation to specific parameter values—flip probability, crop fraction, and rotation angle—for a small CNN trained for approximately 5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST?
gaps.why_open: (Lin et al. 2023) studies augmentation hyperparameter sensitivity for facial expression recognition and finds sensitivity is dataset-dependent, but Fashion-MNIST is not examined. (Shijie et al. 2017) and (Zhang et al. 2015) use fixed augmentation parameters without any sensitivity analysis across parameter values. The noted open problem explicitly states that optimal augmentation hyperparameters are rarely tuned systematically and default values may not be optimal for a given architecture or dataset, yet no paper has characterised this sensitivity for Fashion-MNIST at a short training budget.
gaps.hypothesis: Within the conventional default range (flip probability 0.3–0.7, crop fraction 5–20%, rotation 5–20°), test accuracy varies by less than 0.5% on Fashion-MNIST at 5 epochs indicating defaults are near-optimal; however aggressive values beyond this range such as crop above 25% or rotation above 25° will consistently degrade accuracy by more than 1%.

novelty_check.explanation: None of the prior works perform a systematic sensitivity analysis or factorial grid search over flip probability, crop fraction, and rotation angle as isolated parameters on Fashion-MNIST with a small CNN at ~5 epochs; the closest works apply augmentation as a fixed preprocessing step without ablating individual parameter values.

gaps.compute_needed: 27 conditions × 1 seed × 5 epochs approximately 2–3 GPU hours on Colab T4/L4 potentially requiring multiple sessions
